case.title: Loan #4471 — adverse-action review
case.question: Should the lender deny this application, and if so, what specific principal reason must the adverse-action notice state?

constraints.text: An adverse-action notice must state the specific principal reason(s) for denial; generic or inaccurate statements are non-compliant.
Creditors relying on complex models must still provide specific and accurate reasons; model opacity is not a defense.
The decision must not rely on a prohibited basis or a proxy for one.
Internal policy: applications at or above 45% DTI are declined absent compensating factors.

evidence.summary: Verified gross monthly income is $7,200 (annual $86,400), stable for 3+ years.
Total documented monthly debt obligations are $2,050 (auto $410, cards $340, student $520, proposed mortgage escrowed $780).
Draft worksheet states DTI = 52% and recommends denial for 'excessive DTI'. No computation shown.
Credit score 690; two 30-day late payments in the last 24 months (both on the same card, 14 months ago).
Loan-to-value 82%, within program limits (max 95%).

documents.title: Lending policy excerpt
documents.body: Applications with a debt-to-income ratio at or above 45% are declined absent compensating factors. DTI is computed as total monthly debt obligations divided by gross monthly income. The principal reason stated on any denial must be specific and accurate; template language without case-specific reconciliation is prohibited.

case.question: Should the lender deny this application, and if so, what specific principal reason must the adverse-action notice state?

constraints.text: An adverse-action notice must state the specific principal reason(s) for denial; generic or inaccurate statements are non-compliant.
Creditors relying on complex models must still provide specific and accurate reasons; model opacity is not a defense.

Internal policy: applications at or above 45% DTI are declined absent compensating factors.

revision.answerToStrongestObjection: The objection conflates two distinct problems: what the applicant-facing principal-reason disclosure should say (nothing, since there is no denial) and whether the queued 52%-DTI draft letter gets suppressed operationally. STOP correctly resolves the first. Suppressing the erroneous draft is a case-management/disposition-enforcement control that must exist independent of this disclosure span; if it doesn't, that is a gap in workflow wiring, not a defect curable by stuffing an internal withdrawal instruction into customer-facing text. Doing the latter risks producing exactly the confused, template-like artifact the objection fears, and it would not by itself guarantee suppression either -- only a real enforcement step can do that.
revision.steelmanOfBestRival: The strongest rival case is that this JSON span may be the only artifact anyone reviews before the queued denial letter goes out, and in that world, silence is indistinguishable from 'no objection' to the 52% letter. Given the severity of a false adverse-action notice reaching the applicant and the ECOA/Reg B exposure it creates, a short explicit sentence barring transmission of the unsupported denial reason costs almost nothing and closes that gap on the face of the one record everyone actually reads.
revision.changeMyMind: Evidence that this disclosure span is the sole gating artifact before dispatch -- i.e., no separate disposition-enforcement or human sign-off step exists to block the queued 52%-DTI letter once the file is marked approved. If transmission truly hinges on this span's text alone, I would switch to a short affirmative statement (e.g., candidate barring issuance of any DTI-based denial reason) because the certain harm of a false notice then outweighs the cost of the extra sentence.

case.title: Loan #4471 — adverse-action review
case.question: Should the lender deny this application, and if so, what specific principal reason must the adverse-action notice state?

constraints.text: An adverse-action notice must state the specific principal reason(s) for denial; generic or inaccurate statements are non-compliant.
Creditors relying on complex models must still provide specific and accurate reasons; model opacity is not a defense.
The decision must not rely on a prohibited basis or a proxy for one.
Internal policy: applications at or above 45% DTI are declined absent compensating factors.

evidence.summary: Verified gross monthly income is $7,200 (annual $86,400), stable for 3+ years.
Total documented monthly debt obligations are $2,050 (auto $410, cards $340, student $520, proposed mortgage escrowed $780).
Draft worksheet states DTI = 52% and recommends denial for 'excessive DTI'. No computation shown.
Credit score 690; two 30-day late payments in the last 24 months (both on the same card, 14 months ago).
Loan-to-value 82%, within program limits (max 95%).

documents.title: Lending policy excerpt
documents.body: Applications with a debt-to-income ratio at or above 45% are declined absent compensating factors. DTI is computed as total monthly debt obligations divided by gross monthly income. The principal reason stated on any denial must be specific and accurate; template language without case-specific reconciliation is prohibited.

case.title: Loan #4471 — adverse-action review
case.question: Should the lender deny this application, and if so, what specific principal reason must the adverse-action notice state?

constraints.text: An adverse-action notice must state the specific principal reason(s) for denial; generic or inaccurate statements are non-compliant.
Creditors relying on complex models must still provide specific and accurate reasons; model opacity is not a defense.
The decision must not rely on a prohibited basis or a proxy for one.
Internal policy: applications at or above 45% DTI are declined absent compensating factors.

evidence.summary: Verified gross monthly income is $7,200 (annual $86,400), stable for 3+ years.
Total documented monthly debt obligations are $2,050 (auto $410, cards $340, student $520, proposed mortgage escrowed $780).
Draft worksheet states DTI = 52% and recommends denial for 'excessive DTI'. No computation shown.
Credit score 690; two 30-day late payments in the last 24 months (both on the same card, 14 months ago).
Loan-to-value 82%, within program limits (max 95%).

documents.title: Lending policy excerpt
documents.body: Applications with a debt-to-income ratio at or above 45% are declined absent compensating factors. DTI is computed as total monthly debt obligations divided by gross monthly income. The principal reason stated on any denial must be specific and accurate; template language without case-specific reconciliation is prohibited.
